title: Is Moderate Drinking Healthy? What the Evidence Really Shows
excerpt: Is a drink a day good for you? How the J-curve studies went wrong, what sick-quitter bias and genetic studies revealed, what moderate actually means, and an honest bottom line.
metaDescription: Is moderate drinking healthy? How the old J-curve studies went wrong, what genetic research shows, what moderate means, and an honest bottom line.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** moderate drinking is probably not healthy, but for most adults it is also not very dangerous. For decades, studies seemed to show that people who had a drink or so a day lived longer and had fewer heart attacks than people who never drank. Better research has since chipped away at that idea. Much of the apparent benefit turns out to come from who the comparison group was, not from the alcohol. What's left is a fairly clear picture: the risk from alcohol starts low and rises with every additional drink, the cancer risk has no clear safe floor, and any heart benefit, if it exists at all, is small and limited to some older adults. Drinking a little is a low-risk choice. It just isn't a health habit.

**The quick version of the evidence:** The old "J-curve" (moderate drinkers looking healthier than non-drinkers) is largely explained by "sick quitters" and healthier lifestyles among light drinkers. Genetic studies that sidestep those biases find no heart protection from alcohol. The World Health Organization said in 2023 that no level of drinking is safe for health, and the US Surgeon General's January 2025 advisory highlighted alcohol as a leading preventable cause of cancer. At the same time, the absolute added risk from one drink a day is small for most people. If you drink moderately and enjoy it, you don't need to panic. If you don't drink, there's no health reason to start.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes public research and official guidance. Your own risk depends on your age, sex, family history, medications, and health conditions. **Talk to your doctor** about your drinking if you have high blood pressure, an irregular heartbeat, liver disease, a personal or family history of breast or bowel cancer, depression or anxiety, or you take medicines that interact with alcohol. If you're pregnant or trying to become pregnant, the guidance is not to drink at all. If you're worried that drinking has become hard to control, your doctor is a good place to start, and in the US the free, confidential SAMHSA National Helpline is available any time at **1-800-662-4357**.

## What "Moderate Drinking" Actually Means

Before getting into whether moderate drinking is healthy, it helps to pin down what the term means, because most people picture more than the official definition.

In the US, moderate drinking has traditionally been defined (in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020 to 2025 edition) as **up to 2 drinks a day for men and up to 1 drink a day for women**, on days when alcohol is consumed. That's a ceiling for a given day, not a daily target and not something you can "save up" over the week. The same guidelines also say plainly that drinking less is better for health than drinking more, and that people who don't drink shouldn't start for health reasons.

A "drink" is also smaller than most people think. A US standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which works out to:

- **12 ounces of regular beer** (about 5% alcohol)
- **5 ounces of wine** (about 12% alcohol)
- **1.5 ounces of spirits** (about 40% alcohol, one shot)

A large restaurant pour of wine, a pint of strong IPA, or a generous home-made cocktail can each be closer to two standard drinks. If you've never measured, our guide to [what counts as a standard drink](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) is worth five minutes, because it changes how many drinks most people are actually having.

Other countries draw the line differently, and the trend has been downward:

- **The UK** (Chief Medical Officers' guidelines, 2016) advises both men and women to stay under **14 units a week** (a UK unit is 8 grams of alcohol, so that's roughly 6 pints of average beer or 6 medium glasses of wine), spread over three or more days.
- **Canada** (Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health, 2023) moved to a sliding scale of risk: **2 or fewer standard drinks a week** is described as low risk, **3 to 6** as moderate risk, and **7 or more** as increasingly high risk. Canadian standard drinks are a little smaller than American ones.

So "moderate" is not a scientific boundary where risk switches on. It's a policy line drawn somewhere along a curve that rises steadily. For the other end of the scale, see [how much alcohol is too much](/never-hungover/how-much-alcohol-is-too-much), which covers heavy and binge drinking definitions.

## Where the "Moderate Drinking Is Good for You" Idea Came From

The belief that a drink a day is healthy didn't come from nowhere. For decades, large observational studies (studies that follow groups of people over time and compare outcomes, without assigning anyone to drink or not drink) kept finding the same pattern.

When researchers plotted death rates against how much people drank, the graph looked like the letter J. Non-drinkers sat a little higher on the left. Light and moderate drinkers dipped lower, suggesting they lived longer. Then the line climbed steeply as drinking went up. Heart disease showed a similar dip. This became known as the **J-curve**, and it was repeated in study after study across many countries.

On top of that, there was a plausible mechanism. Alcohol raises HDL ("good") cholesterol and has mild blood-thinning effects. The "French paradox" (the observation that French people ate a rich diet but had relatively low heart disease rates) added a cultural story about red wine. By the 1990s, "a glass of wine is good for your heart" had become common wisdom, repeated by doctors and in the press.

The problem is that observational studies can show that two things go together, not that one causes the other. And in the case of moderate drinking, there turned out to be several strong reasons why moderate drinkers might look healthier even if alcohol itself does nothing good.

## Problem One: The "Sick Quitter" Bias

The biggest flaw in the old studies was the comparison group.

Many studies lumped everyone who didn't currently drink into one "non-drinker" group. But that group included **former drinkers**, and many former drinkers stopped *because* they were already unwell. Someone diagnosed with heart disease, diabetes, liver disease, or cancer is often told to stop drinking. Someone who had a drinking problem may have quit. People on certain medications avoid alcohol. All of them get counted as "non-drinkers," and all of them are, on average, sicker than the general population.

The British epidemiologist Gerry Shaper and colleagues described this in the Lancet in 1988 and called it the **"sick quitter" hypothesis**. If your non-drinking comparison group is loaded with people who quit because they were ill, moderate drinkers will look healthier by comparison, even if alcohol has no benefit at all.

There's a second, related issue. Some people who report light drinking at the start of a study were heavier drinkers in the past, and some people who report "occasional" drinking really drink less because of health problems. People's drinking also changes over their lives, while many studies measured it only once.

When researchers have gone back and tried to fix these problems, the J-curve mostly flattens. The best-known effort is a series of meta-analyses (studies that pool the results of many other studies) led by Tim Stockwell at the Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research. A 2016 analysis in the *Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs* pooled 87 studies and found that once former drinkers were separated out and study quality was taken into account, low-volume drinkers no longer showed a clear survival advantage. An updated 2023 analysis in *JAMA Network Open*, covering 107 cohort studies and several million people, reached the same conclusion: occasional and low-volume drinking was not associated with lower risk of death compared with lifetime non-drinkers, while risk rose at higher levels of drinking, and at lower thresholds for women than for men.

## Problem Two: Moderate Drinkers Tend to Have Healthier Lives Anyway

Even after removing sick quitters, moderate drinkers in many countries differ from lifelong non-drinkers in ways that have nothing to do with alcohol.

In many Western populations, people who drink a moderate amount tend, on average, to have higher incomes, more education, better access to healthcare, more social connection, and healthier diets than lifelong abstainers. Some lifelong non-drinkers avoid alcohol for reasons linked to poorer health or lower income. Researchers call this **confounding**: a third factor (wealth, education, overall lifestyle) affects both drinking habits and health, making it look like one causes the other.

Studies try to adjust for these factors statistically, but adjustment is never perfect. You can't fully measure "lives a generally comfortable, health-conscious life" with a few survey questions. Even small amounts of leftover confounding are enough to create the modest dip seen in the J-curve.

One telling sign: moderate drinking in some older studies appeared to protect against things alcohol has no plausible way to affect, such as hip fractures, hearing loss, or even dying in an accident. When a "treatment" seems to protect against everything, the more likely explanation is that the people taking it were healthier to begin with.

## Problem Three: Raising HDL Doesn't Seem to Protect the Heart

The main biological argument for alcohol's heart benefit was that it raises HDL cholesterol. That is true. Alcohol does nudge HDL up.

But later research weakened the idea that raising HDL by itself protects the heart. A large genetic study published in the Lancet in 2012 (Voight and colleagues) found that people born with gene variants that raise HDL did not have lower heart attack risk. Several drug trials of medicines that raise HDL have also failed to prevent heart attacks. So "alcohol raises good cholesterol" no longer translates cleanly into "alcohol protects your heart." Alcohol also raises blood pressure and triglycerides, which push the other way.

## The Genetic Studies: Mendelian Randomization

The strongest way to test whether something causes a health effect is a randomized trial, where people are randomly assigned to do it or not. Nobody has ever run a long-term randomized trial of moderate drinking versus abstaining that is large enough to measure heart attacks or deaths. A planned US trial (the Moderate Alcohol and Cardiovascular Health trial) was shut down by the National Institutes of Health in 2018 over concerns about its funding from the alcohol industry.

So researchers have turned to a clever workaround called **Mendelian randomization**. Some people inherit gene variants that change how they process alcohol. Because genes are handed out more or less at random at conception, these variants act like a natural experiment. People with variants that make alcohol unpleasant tend to drink less for their whole lives, and they aren't otherwise richer, sicker, or more health-conscious than everyone else. Comparing them to people without the variants gives a cleaner look at what alcohol itself does.

The results have not been kind to the J-curve:

- **A 2014 study in the BMJ** (Holmes and colleagues) pooled data from dozens of studies on a variant of the ADH1B gene that is linked to drinking less. Carriers drank less alcohol and had **lower** risk of coronary heart disease, along with lower blood pressure and body mass index. That's the opposite of what you'd expect if moderate drinking protected the heart. The authors concluded that reducing alcohol is likely to benefit heart health, even for light-to-moderate drinkers.
- **A 2019 study in the Lancet** (Millwood and colleagues) used the China Kadoorie Biobank, which follows hundreds of thousands of adults in China. Many East Asian people carry variants in the ALDH2 and ADH1B genes that cause flushing and discomfort with alcohol, which strongly reduces how much they drink. Using these variants, the researchers found that **stroke risk rose steadily with alcohol intake**, with no protective effect at moderate levels. The apparent protection seen in ordinary observational analysis disappeared when the genetic approach was used.
- **A 2022 study in JAMA Network Open** (Biddinger and colleagues) used the UK Biobank and found that light drinkers tended to have healthier lifestyles than abstainers, and that in the genetic analysis, alcohol intake at all levels was linked to higher cardiovascular risk. The risk was small at low levels and rose much more steeply at higher ones.

Mendelian randomization has its own limits. It assumes the gene affects health only through drinking, and it estimates the effect of lifelong differences in drinking rather than a choice you make at 50. But it removes the sick-quitter and lifestyle problems that dogged the old studies, and it keeps pointing the same direction.

## What Major Health Authorities Say Now

Official guidance has shifted a lot in the past decade.

**The Global Burden of Disease study.** A large analysis published in the Lancet in 2018 concluded that the level of drinking that minimized overall health loss was zero drinks per week. A follow-up published in 2022 added nuance. It found that risk varies by age and region: for adults under 40, there was no health benefit from drinking and the risks were higher, while some adults over 40 without other health problems might see a small benefit from very low amounts, driven mainly by heart disease. Even in that more generous reading, the "beneficial" amount was well under one drink a day.

**The World Health Organization.** In January 2023, the WHO's European office published a statement in *Lancet Public Health* saying that **no level of alcohol consumption is safe for health**, mainly because of cancer risk. The point wasn't that one drink is deadly. It was that researchers can't identify a threshold below which cancer risk stops rising.

**The US Surgeon General.** In January 2025, the Surgeon General issued an advisory on alcohol and cancer risk. It described alcohol as the third-leading preventable cause of cancer in the US after tobacco and obesity, noted that most Americans aren't aware of the link, and called for updating the health warning on alcohol labels to mention cancer.

**The National Academies.** Not every recent report points the same way. A December 2024 review by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, commissioned to inform the US dietary guidelines, concluded with moderate certainty that moderate drinkers had a somewhat lower risk of death from all causes than people who had never drunk, while also finding that moderate drinking was linked to a higher risk of breast cancer. Its authors noted the evidence base was limited. This is worth knowing, because it shows the debate isn't fully settled, and honest experts still disagree about how much of the old J-curve survives once biases are dealt with.

The fair summary: nearly everyone agrees that risk rises as drinking rises, that alcohol causes cancer, and that nobody should start drinking for their health. The live disagreement is about whether a very small amount carries a tiny net benefit for some older adults, or a tiny net harm.

## The Risks That Don't Go Away at Moderate Levels

Even people who still believe in a small heart benefit agree that some risks rise from the very first drink.

### Cancer

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies alcoholic drinks as a Group 1 carcinogen, the category for agents with the strongest evidence that they cause cancer in humans. Alcohol is linked to at least seven cancers: mouth, throat, voice box, esophagus, liver, colon and rectum, and breast.

The main reason is **acetaldehyde**, the chemical your body makes when it breaks down alcohol. It damages DNA and interferes with the body's ability to repair it. Alcohol also raises estrogen levels, which is part of why breast cancer risk climbs even at low levels of drinking. For breast cancer in particular, studies consistently find that risk rises measurably with each additional daily drink, with no clear safe threshold.

It's important to keep the scale in mind. For an individual woman, going from zero to one drink a day raises her lifetime breast cancer risk by a small amount in absolute terms. But "small" is not "none," and across a whole population, it adds up to a lot of cases.

### Blood pressure and heart rhythm

Alcohol raises blood pressure, and the effect grows with the amount. Regular drinking is one of the more common, fixable causes of high blood pressure.

It's also linked to **atrial fibrillation**, an irregular heartbeat that raises stroke risk. A large 2021 analysis in the *European Heart Journal* (Csengeri and colleagues), pooling data from several European cohorts, found that even around one drink a day was associated with a higher risk of developing atrial fibrillation compared with not drinking. Our [guide to alcohol and heart health](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-heart-health-complete-cardiovascular-guide-2025) covers the cardiovascular picture in more detail.

### The brain

A 2017 study in the BMJ (Topiwala and colleagues), which followed British civil servants for 30 years, found that even moderate drinking was associated with shrinkage in the hippocampus, a part of the brain important for memory. A 2022 study in *Nature Communications* (Daviet and colleagues), using brain scans from the UK Biobank, found that drinking was linked to smaller brain volume, with differences visible even at one to two drinks a day. These are observational studies, so they can't prove cause, but they don't support the idea that light drinking is good for the brain.

### Sleep, mood, and everyday effects

Even when it doesn't show up in mortality statistics, a nightly drink or two can make sleep lighter and more broken in the second half of the night, worsen acid reflux, and for some people, worsen anxiety the next day. These effects are reversible, but they matter for how you feel day to day. We cover the cumulative effects of a daily habit in [is drinking every day bad?](/never-hungover/is-drinking-every-day-bad).

## Does the Type of Drink Matter?

The red wine story deserves a short answer: there is no good evidence that red wine is healthier than other drinks once you account for who drinks it. Red wine contains resveratrol and other polyphenols that look interesting in lab studies, but the amounts in a glass are tiny compared to the doses used in those experiments, and human studies of resveratrol supplements haven't shown clear heart benefits. Wine drinkers, in many countries, also tend to be wealthier and eat better than beer or spirits drinkers, which helps explain why they look healthier in observational data. We go through the details in [is red wine good for you?](/never-hungover/is-red-wine-good-for-you).

What clearly matters more than the type of drink is **how much and how fast**. The ethanol is the same molecule in beer, wine, and spirits. Five drinks on a Saturday is not the same as one drink on each of five nights, even though the weekly total matches. Binge-style drinking (in the US, roughly 4 or more drinks for women or 5 or more for men in about two hours) is linked to accidents, injuries, heart rhythm problems, and worse hangovers, and it erases any theoretical benefit of moderate drinking.

## So Who Might Still Benefit, and Who Should Be Most Careful?

Putting everything together, here's a fair reading of who sits where.

**People for whom any heart benefit is least likely and risks are highest:**

- **Adults under about 40**, whose risk of heart disease is low to begin with and whose risk from injuries and accidents is higher
- **Women with a family history of breast cancer**
- People with **high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, liver disease, or a history of stroke**
- People taking **medicines that interact with alcohol**, such as sedatives, some pain medicines, some antidepressants, and blood thinners (check with your prescriber or pharmacist about your specific medicines)
- Anyone who is **pregnant or trying to conceive**
- People who find it **hard to stop at one or two**, or who have a family history of alcohol problems

**People for whom moderate drinking is lowest risk:**

- Older adults who are otherwise healthy, drink small amounts with food, never binge, and don't have the conditions above. Even here, the most generous recent analyses describe at most a small benefit, and other experts think it's zero.

That last group shouldn't take this as a prescription. Exercise, not smoking, blood pressure control, and a good diet each do far more for the heart than a glass of wine could, without the cancer trade-off.

## A Practical Way to Think About It

Here's a simple frame that fits the evidence without catastrophizing.

1. **Don't drink for your health.** No major health body recommends starting to drink for health reasons. If you don't drink, you're not missing out on anything medically.
2. **If you drink, less is better.** Risk rises along a curve. Going from 10 drinks a week to 5 lowers your risk more than going from 2 to 0, but both move in the right direction.
3. **Avoid binges.** Spreading drinks out and staying at one or two on any given day avoids the sharpest risks.
4. **Have drink-free days.** Several alcohol-free days a week help keep tolerance low and make it easier to notice if the habit is creeping up.
5. **Measure your pours.** Most people underestimate how much they drink because home and restaurant servings are larger than a standard drink.
6. **Know your personal risk factors.** Family history, blood pressure, heart rhythm, and medications change the math more than anything in this article.

If you're curious what cutting back feels like, a month off or a few weeks of drinking less is a low-stakes experiment. Many people notice better sleep and steadier energy. Our [sober-curious guide](/never-hungover/sober-curious) covers how people approach that without making it an all-or-nothing decision.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Because this site covers hangover and liver-support supplements, it's worth being clear about what they can and can't do here.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. Some people find it helps them feel better the morning after drinking. That's the most anyone can honestly say for it.

What DHM does **not** do is make drinking healthier. There is no good evidence that it lowers alcohol's cancer risk, its effect on blood pressure, or its effect on heart rhythm. Acetaldehyde still forms, and the risks described above still apply. Think of it, at most, as something that may make an occasional night out a little easier on how you feel the next day, not as a way to offset the long-term risks of drinking.

If you do want to try it for occasional use, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side. If you take prescription medicines, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Moderate drinking isn't the health habit it was once sold as. The evidence that made it look protective came mostly from flawed comparisons, especially the "sick quitter" problem and the healthier lifestyles of moderate drinkers. Genetic studies that avoid those biases find no heart protection, and the cancer risk rises from the first drink with no clear safe floor. That's why the WHO says no level is safe and why the Surgeon General has called for cancer warnings on alcohol.

At the same time, the added risk from a drink or so a day is small for most healthy adults, and some respected reviews still find a modest mortality advantage for moderate drinkers. The honest conclusion sits between the headlines: a little alcohol is a low-risk choice you can make for enjoyment, not a health choice you should make for your heart. If you drink, less is better, binges are the part to avoid, and your own health history matters more than any average. If you don't drink, don't start.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is moderate drinking good for your heart?**

Probably not, at least not in the way older studies suggested. Those studies compared moderate drinkers with a non-drinking group that included many people who had quit because they were ill, which made moderate drinkers look healthier. Genetic studies that avoid this problem have found no heart protection from alcohol, and alcohol raises blood pressure and the risk of atrial fibrillation. Some researchers still think a very small benefit may exist for some older adults, but exercise, blood pressure control, and not smoking do far more for the heart.

**How much alcohol is considered moderate drinking?**

In the US, moderate drinking has traditionally meant up to 2 standard drinks a day for men and up to 1 for women, on days when alcohol is consumed. A standard drink is about 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits. Other countries set lower limits: the UK advises under 14 units a week for everyone, and Canada's 2023 guidance describes 2 or fewer drinks a week as low risk.

**Is there a safe amount of alcohol?**

The World Health Organization said in 2023 that no level of drinking is safe for health, mainly because cancer risk rises from the first drink with no clear threshold. That doesn't mean one drink is dangerous. It means risk starts low and rises steadily with the amount, so there's no level that is completely risk-free. For most healthy adults, the added risk from light drinking is small.

**What is the sick quitter effect?**

It's a bias in older alcohol studies. Many studies counted former drinkers as non-drinkers, but a lot of former drinkers stopped because they were already sick, for example after a diagnosis of heart disease or diabetes. That made the non-drinking group look less healthy and made moderate drinkers look better by comparison. When researchers separate former drinkers from lifelong non-drinkers, most of the apparent benefit of moderate drinking shrinks or disappears.

**Is red wine healthier than beer or spirits?**

There's no good evidence that it is once you account for who drinks it. Red wine contains resveratrol, but a glass holds far less than the amounts used in lab studies, and wine drinkers tend to be wealthier and eat better than other drinkers, which explains much of the apparent advantage. The alcohol itself is the same molecule in every drink, and it carries the same risks.

**Should I stop drinking if I only drink moderately?**

That's a personal decision, and the evidence doesn't say moderate drinkers are in danger. If you enjoy a drink and have no risk factors, drinking less and avoiding binges captures most of the benefit. If you have high blood pressure, an irregular heartbeat, liver disease, a family history of breast cancer, or take medicines that interact with alcohol, talk to your doctor about whether cutting back or stopping makes sense for you.

**Can a supplement like DHM make moderate drinking healthier?**

No. DHM has promising early research on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly from animal studies, and some people find it helps with how they feel the next morning. But there is no good evidence that it reduces alcohol's cancer, blood pressure, or heart rhythm risks. It is not a way to offset the long-term effects of drinking.
